SK1083 Use foreach over an indexed for

A for over 0..Count whose index is only ever used to index that one collection is a foreach written the long way.

CategoryModernization
Default severitysuggestion
ScopeSemantic
Needs a compilationyes
Runs under --load=looseno
Cached per fileyes
Fixyes, review it
Language version floor—
Since2.0
ReSharperForCanBeConvertedToForeach (resharper_for_can_be_converted_to_foreach_highlighting)

Why

The index in this loop is not information. It is not printed, not compared, not passed anywhere and not used to reach a second collection — it exists to move a cursor the language already knows how to move. What the long form adds is three places to make an off-by-one error, in the bound, in the comparison operator and in the increment, and every one of them is silent. foreach deletes all three. It is a shape a model writes far more often than a person does, because the indexed loop is what most of the code written before foreach became the default looks like.

Example

Instead of:

for (var i = 0; i < entries.Count; i++) {
    Process(entries[i]);
}

Write:

foreach (var entry in entries) {
    Process(entry);
}

When it does not fire

⚠ Three facts are proved before anything is reported, and the rule is silent rather than clever when any of them is not decidable. One: the loop runs the whole range in steps of one — a single int i = 0 declarator, a condition that is exactly i < receiver.Count or i < receiver.Length against the same receiver the body indexes, and an incrementor that is exactly i++ or ++i. <=, a bound that is an expression rather than that receiver's own count, a second declarator, a comma-separated incrementor and a for whose body assigns to i are all excluded, because each one makes "visits every element once, in order" a claim rather than a reading. Two: the index is used only as receiver[i]; any other appearance of i in the body — arithmetic on it, a second collection indexed by it, passing it to a method — withdraws the finding, because the element alone does not carry it. Three: the collection is not touched in the body except through those reads. Any other reference to the receiver's symbol inside the loop suppresses the finding, which is the same guard SK4006 uses and it is deliberately blunt: a body that calls list.Add, passes the list on, or reassigns it is a body this rule cannot reason about. ⚠ The receiver must be an array, a `string`, a `List<T>` or an `ImmutableList<T>` — types whose enumerator is documented to yield element 0 through element Count - 1 in that order. An IList<T> or a hand-written indexable type promises no such thing, and a foreach over one could visit a different sequence entirely. ⚠ The residual risk, and the reason `fixIsSafe` is false, is mutation the rule cannot see. A for over a List<T> that is mutated through a method call in the body keeps running where a foreach throws InvalidOperationException; the receiver is required to be a local or a parameter to shrink that surface, but proving that no call reached the list is not decidable and is not attempted. Arrays are immune — they have no version field — and are the case where the fix is in practice mechanical. ⚠ The rule needs a name for the element that nothing else uses, and the obvious scoping guards are both blind to the case that matters. The new variable is declared in the header and its scope is the body, so what collides with it is what the loop itself declares: LookupSymbols at the loop's start position cannot see a pattern variable scoped to an if inside the body, and the member-wide scan skips every node overlapping the span being moved — which is the whole loop. Serilog's MessageTemplate.GetElementsOfTypeToArray is the case that found it: it loops over tokens and its body writes if (tokens[i] is TResult token), so the obvious name was taken and the fix produced CS0136. A third scan over the loop's own declarations is what stops it, and the rule falls through to item or stays silent when it cannot pick a name. ⚠ Comments and preprocessor directives inside the for header exclude the loop, because the fix replaces the whole header. ⚠ It interacts with SK4001 in the opposite direction to SK1084: foreach over a List<T> uses a struct enumerator and allocates nothing, so this rewrite adds no LINQ and no allocation to a hot path, and the two rules do not disagree.
